mental.resume: Keep a cool head, know what to do first, decide whether to stay or go.

p: In most survival situations, it is neither cold nor hunger that tips things over, but panic: you rush, you scatter your efforts, you take a wrong direction, you forget to eat or to shelter.
So the first reflex to learn is to slow down. A situation that seems catastrophic often becomes manageable as soon as you break it into small, simple problems, dealt with in the right order.

etapes: Stop: don't move, sit down, take a sip of water, breathe slowly.
Think: what happened? What is really urgent? Who knows where I am?
Observe: the surroundings (shelter, water, wood, dangers), the weather, the time of sunset, your gear, your physical state.
Plan: decide only the next 2 or 3 actions, then act calmly.

encadre.texte: Stopping for five minutes never wastes time. Setting off in the wrong direction does.

p: The rule of 3 gives the logical order: you die in 3 minutes without air, in 3 hours without protection in cold, wet weather, in 3 days without water and in 3 weeks without food. In practice, in our climates:
etapes: Life-threatening emergencies: bleeding, serious injury, unconscious person (see First aid).
Protect yourself from cold and wet: dry clothes, shelter, insulation from the ground.
Signal and alert the emergency services if needed.
Water: find it and make it safe to drink.
Fire: warmth, morale, boiled water, signal.
Food, last: it is almost never the emergency.

p: If someone knows your route and your return time, staying put is almost always the best decision: rescuers search around the planned route first, and a person who is still and visible is found much faster.

Leaving is justified if the place is dangerous (flood, falling rocks, extreme cold with no possible shelter), if nobody will look for you, or if you know exactly where to go and can get there before nightfall.

encadre.texte: If you leave, leave a clearly visible message (branches forming an arrow, a note under a stone) showing your direction and the time.

p: Crossing this stream, going down this steep slope, walking another hour before dark: each decision is weighed with two simple questions. How likely is it to go wrong? And if it goes wrong, how serious is it?
liste: Likely AND serious (crossing a river in flood): give up.
Unlikely but serious (camping under a dead tree in strong wind): choose another option, it is often easy.
Likely but minor (getting your feet wet): accept it, with a plan to deal with it (dry socks).
Every precaution has a cost (time, energy, weight): choose it according to the real risk, not fear.

encadre.texte: Fatigue, lack of sleep, cold, hunger, dehydration and the urge to “finish anyway” (especially in a group) lead to bad decisions. If you recognise one of them, slow down and choose the most cautious option.

liste: Set small, achievable goals: gather wood, then put up the shelter, then boil the water.
Keep a routine: eat at set times, tidy your camp, tend the fire.
Talk (out loud if need be), sing, write down what you do: it keeps the mind busy and helps you think.
Look after yourself: a washed face, dry feet, a hot drink change everything.
In a group: share out roles, make decisions together, watch over the most vulnerable.

p: In a disaster, rescuers go first to the most serious situations. During the first days, every household must be able to cope on its own: this has been the European Union's recommendation since 2025, confirmed in November 2026.

etapes: Get informed: your country's alert system, radio, official sources.
Make a plan: contacts, meeting point, everyone's role.
Build up the home stock and the evacuation bag, little by little.

encadre.texte: Today > Ready 72 h: your household, your calculated kit, your stock with dates and your family plan, all working offline.

preparer.resume: Route, someone to tell, pocket survival kit, clothing: 90% of safety is decided before you leave.

p: This is the most important rule in this whole guide. Before each trip, give a loved one: your planned route, where you will sleep, your return time, and the time after which they should call the emergency services if they haven't heard from you.

encadre.texte: One person who knows where you are is worth more than all the gear in the world.

liste: Check the rules of the place: bivouac allowed, fires, protected areas (see the Law and ethics chapter).
Locate water points, escape routes (roads, villages) and areas without signal.
Check the weather the day before and on the day, and the time of sunset (Bivouac tab).
Allow plenty of time: you move more slowly than you think with a loaded pack, in a forest or at night.
Keep the map cached in Bivaska and take a paper map.

p: A small waterproof case that never leaves your pocket or belt, even for a short walk. If it is in the pack and the pack is lost, it is useless.
liste: Lighter + fire steel (ferrocerium) + a few fire starters
Survival blanket
Whistle
Small torch or head torch
Knife or multi-tool
5 m of strong cord
Water purification tablets
A few plasters, dressings and a tick remover
An energy bar
A pencil and waterproof paper

p: The body cools quickly when it is wet, from rain or from sweat. Rather than one big garment, you stack layers that you take off and put back on according to effort and weather.
etapes: Base layer next to the skin: merino wool or synthetic, never cotton (it holds moisture and chills you).
Warm layer: fleece or down jacket.
Shell: waterproof and windproof jacket and trousers.

encadre.texte: Take off a layer BEFORE you sweat going uphill, put it back on AS SOON as you stop. Keep a dry outfit in a waterproof bag, for the night only.

liste: Cotton: pleasant when dry, but it holds water and chills you as soon as it is wet. Avoid it in cool, damp weather.
Wool (merino): warm even when a little damp, doesn't hold odours. Ideal as a base layer and for socks.
Fleece: light, dries quickly, warm even when damp, but lets the wind through.
Down (feathers): the best warmth-to-weight ratio… as long as it stays dry. Wet, it hardly warms at all.
Synthetic (polyester wadding): a little heavier than down, but keeps a good part of its warmth when damp. The right choice in our rainy climates.
Waterproof breathable membranes: block rain and wind while letting some vapour out. Open the vents during effort.

p: The full checklist, editable and with your photos, is in the Bivouac tab. The essentials: shelter (tent or tarp), sleeping system suited to the night temperature, insulating mat, stove, water, head torch, first-aid kit, charged phone and power bank.

campement.resume: Choosing the spot, organising your camp, sleeping warm and dry.

p: Setting up camp at night, in the rain and tired, is the best way to sleep badly and put yourself in danger. Plan to arrive at least 1 h 30 before sunset (shown in the Bivouac tab). In winter, night sometimes falls before 5 pm.

liste: Legal: bivouac area, private land with permission, or an area where bivouacking is tolerated.
Above you: no dead branch and no dead or leaning tree. These branches fall without warning, especially in wind.
Under you: flat ground, without roots or stones, slightly domed so that water runs off. Not in a hollow.
Around: not at the bottom of a valley (cold air sinks there at night) nor right at the edge of a river (damp, rising water).
Sheltered from the prevailing wind by terrain, a copse or a rock.
Not on a game trail, near a burrow or a wasps' or processionary caterpillars' nest.
More than 50 m from water, to protect it and not disturb the animals that come to drink.

p: Before putting down your pack, two minutes of observation avoid most bivouac accidents: a dead branch above the shelter, a stream that can rise, a hollow where cold air collects, a wild boar path. The sheet “Spotting the dangers of the camp” details each point.

encadre.texte: A dead branch can fall without a breath of wind. Never sleep under dead wood, even for a single night.

p: A well-organised camp means less lost gear and fewer accidents. Place the areas relative to each other, taking the wind into account:
liste: Sleeping area: upwind, away from smoke.
Fire and cooking area (if allowed): downwind, at least 3 m from the tent.
Wood store: within reach of the fire but not too close, sheltered from rain.
Water area: bottles and boiled water kept apart from raw water, so you never mix them up.
Toilets: more than 50 m from the camp and the water, downwind.
Food: closed, hung or stored outside the tent at night (wild boar, foxes, rodents).

encadre.texte: Always keep head torch, knife and water bottle in the same place in the tent: you'll find them in the dark.

etapes: Insulate from the ground: cold ground draws away your heat much faster than air. An insulating mat, or failing that 20 to 30 cm of dead leaves, ferns or dry needles.
Eat a fatty, sugary meal before sleeping: the body produces heat while digesting.
Have a hot drink, then go to the toilet before bed: a full bladder cools you down.
Sleep with a hat, dry socks and the dry outfit kept for the night.
Slip a well-closed bottle of hot water into the sleeping bag (hot-water bottle).
Never sleep in the damp clothes of the day.

p: Military cold-weather manuals sum up the art of staying warm in four letters:
liste: C, clean: dirt and grease crush the air pockets in clothing, which then insulates less well.
O, avoid overheating: open up and remove a layer as soon as you sweat, because sweat chills you as it dries.
L, loose and in layers: nothing tight, several thin layers rather than one thick one.
D, dry: protect your clothes from water, dry socks and gloves against your body or on your pack.

p: Damp is enemy number one when bivouacking in our climates. Condensation forms inside the tent when the warm, moist air of your breath touches the cold fabric.
liste: Keep a vent open, even in cold weather.
Don't cook or dry clothes in the tent.
Wipe off condensation in the morning with a small cloth.
Let the sleeping bag dry in the sun or air as soon as possible.

p: In the morning, take things down in reverse order, check that the fire is completely out, take everything with you, and leave the spot as you found it: grass straightened, leaves scattered. The best bivouac is one whose existence nobody can guess.

In Belgium and neighbouring countries, night visitors are foxes, wild boar, martens and above all mice. They come for food and smells. Anything edible or scented (toothpaste included) goes in a closed bag, hung away from where you sleep. A wild boar won't attack a camper, but it will turn your pack over if it smells a meal.
In the rain, put up the roof first, settle underneath, then change into dry clothes straight away. Wet clothes go back on the next day for walking: the night outfit must stay dry, whatever it takes.
